docs.title: VMware to OpenShift Virtualization
docs.text:
Welcome, and thank you for joining us. Today you move a real Windows + PostgreSQL VM from VMware onto OpenShift Virtualization, between two clusters and through a disaster-recovery failover, and prove with your own data that nothing was lost. Everything happens in your web browser: this site is all you need.

Begin: Lab 0 Read the student guide

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1 · Get your login

Your instructor gives you one username and password. It opens everything: vCenter, both OpenShift clusters, your Windows VM and its database.

2 · Read the student guide

The student guide explains how the class works and lists the demos in order, with their times.

3 · Do Lab 0

Lab 0 takes about 5 minutes: sign in, open a command line, reach your VM's database.

Stuck, or something not working? Ask your instructor.

They can reset your login, catch you up, or show any step on the big screen. Stuck for five minutes means ask. See Get help for everything else.

docs.title: What you will do today
docs.text:
• Sign in once and reach vCenter and two OpenShift clusters with the same account
  • Migrate your own Windows + PostgreSQL VM from vSphere to OpenShift Virtualization, cold and warm
  • Go deeper if your class does: disaster recovery, backup and restore, moving between clusters
  • Prove with your own data that nothing was lost, changed or reordered on any move
  • Bonus rounds for early finishers: live migration, snapshot restore, a hostile disaster-recovery failover

docs.title: How the class works
docs.text:
• One VM each: win-pg-s<NN>, a full copy of the instructor's, in your own vCenter folder, at its own address.
  • One namespace each on both clusters, named your class ID. You are admin there.
  • One password everywhere.
  • Only a web browser: nothing to install. Commands run in a terminal inside the OpenShift console.
  • Every step: inject your data → change something → verify it all arrived. Each demo ends by reading your rows back with chain_ok = t: that is your evidence.
  • 🧑‍🏫 marks a step only the instructor runs. [verify] marks a step still being proven: if it fails, ask.
  • 🎬 every section has a recording of the same steps in the console: watch it, then do it.

docs.title: Kubernetes in a few ideas
docs.text:
A cluster. A set of machines (nodes) run as one computer. The control plane keeps the desired state; the worker nodes run the workloads, your VMs included. One API serves everything: the web console, oc and automation. OpenShift is Kubernetes plus an installer, a console, security defaults and operators, supported by Red Hat. Each of our two clusters has 4 nodes.

You declare it; controllers make it so. Everything is an object in YAML: what you want (spec) and what is true now (status). Controllers keep comparing the two and act until they match. An operator is a controller with its own object types. Today's: OpenShift Virtualization (VMs), MTV (migrations), ODF (storage), NMState (host networking), ACM (many clusters). You don't run "migrate" as a command: you create a migration Plan, and MTV does the work and reports progress in its status.

A VM is a pod. A pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes schedules. OpenShift Virtualization runs each VM's QEMU/KVM inside a pod (virt-launcher-<vm>): VirtualMachine is the definition, VirtualMachineInstance the running VM. So VMs and containers share one scheduler, network, storage and set of permissions. Live migration is a new pod on another node, with the memory copied across.

Namespaces and RBAC. A namespace groups objects and is where permissions apply, like a vCenter folder with its own permissions. RBAC binds roles (what you may do) to users and groups (who).

Storage. A VM disk is a PersistentVolumeClaim ("I need 10 GiB like this"). A StorageClass says how claims are met, through a CSI driver. Site A runs ODF (Ceph, on the lab's SSDs: snapshots, clones and replication for disaster recovery); site B runs NFS for now.

Networking. Every pod gets an address on the pod network; a Service gives a stable name. NMState builds a bridge for a lab VLAN on each node, and a NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) puts a VM's NIC on it. So your migrated VM keeps its address.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
• In class: ask your instructor. Stuck for five minutes means ask; nobody is graded on getting stuck. They can reset your login, catch you up, or show any step on the big screen.
  • A step fails: every section has a 🎬 recording of the same steps. Watch it while the instructor looks at your lab. A step marked [verify] is still being proven: tell the instructor rather than improvising.
  • Your login doesn't work: your instructor can reset it. Don't keep retrying: repeated wrong tries can lock the account for a while.
  • A page is stuck after a timeout: sign in again in a private window. Nothing is lost: your VM, your data and your terminal live in the lab, not in the browser.
  • no pg_hba.conf entry … user "student-01": the database login uses an underscore, student_01, not the hyphen of your class ID. Type it again with _. It is not a network fault.
  • The OpenShift console goes dark but vCenter still opens: your computer is asking a public DNS server (such as 8.8.8.8) for the lab's names and gets a dead address. Turn off your browser's Secure DNS (DNS over HTTPS) and tell the instructor, who can point your laptop at the lab's DNS.
  • After class: the lab team, at lab@paragonmicro.com.

This site is public and never contains passwords or anything about your company's environment.

docs.text: Version 0.9.1 · draft · 2026-10-14 · class/student-guide.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
You take a real Windows Server + PostgreSQL VM from VMware vSphere onto Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization, cold and then warm. You move it between two OpenShift clusters and protect it with OpenShift Data Foundation disaster recovery. At every step you write your own data into the VM's database and prove that none of it was lost, changed or reordered.

This guide is the map. The steps are in the demo guides below.

docs.title: Your login, and what you need
docs.text:
The instructor gives you your login. One student username and one password open everything in this class:

Resource Sign in as vSphere Client (vCenter) and both OpenShift consoles your class ID, with SSO (Entra) Your Windows VM .\student-NN Your VM's PostgreSQL database student_NN

All you need is a web browser. Nothing is installed on your computer. You work in the vSphere Client, the two OpenShift consoles, and your browser terminal: a shell in your own pod in the OpenShift console, where every command in these guides runs. Copy a command here with its copy button; paste it there with right-click → Paste.

Lab 0 walks you through it in about 5 minutes: open the tabs, sign in to vCenter, both OpenShift clusters and PostgreSQL, and see your VM and your access.

💡 A page stuck after a timeout? Sign in again in a private window. Nothing is lost: your VM, your data and your terminal live in the lab, not in the browser.

docs.title: How the lab is put together
docs.text:
Each class gets its own three environments (lab diagram):

Environment What it is You vSphere vCenter + ESXi, where your VM starts inspect your VM, enable CBT, shut it down Site A OpenShift + OpenShift Virtualization + MTV, on ODF storage migrate your VM in, run it, snapshot it Site B the same on NFS storage, plus the ACM / DR hub move your VM in, fail over to it

The zone names (lz1, ocp-lz1, …) change per booking; the guides use them as examples. Your browser terminal already knows your own (type ovedr).

  • Your own VM, win-pg-s<NN>: a full copy of the instructor's, with its own address, in your own vCenter folder. You power it, snapshot it, migrate it and fail it over yourself.
  • Your own namespace on both clusters, named your class ID, where you are admin. Your VM lands there, and your browser terminal lives there.
  • Everything is staged; you do the last step. Each demo's pieces (operators, maps, a migration plan for your VM) are pre-built, and each guide shows how to build them yourself (Lab S). Your task is to review and start.

docs.title: Lab 0: Access and tools
docs.text:
Version 1.1.0 · draft · 2026-10-13 · class/demos/00-access-and-tools.md

About 5 minutes. You sign in to the lab in your browser, open a command line, and prove you can reach the cluster and your own VM's database. One recording covers the whole lab: watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

🎬 Video: Lab 0: Access and tools

🎬 Lab 0: Access and tools: a recording of the whole lab, done in the browser (3 min 47 s). Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

You need your class ID and password from the instructor (one login for everything), and your booking's three addresses. The instructor gives you N, A and B; the examples below use 1, ocp-lz1 and ocp-lz2.

Your names, by example. The examples in this lab are for student-01 on booking 0024-012. Swap in your own:

What Example Where it comes from Class ID (also your project) student-01-0024-012 your sign-in name, the part before @ Your VM win-pg-s01 s + your student number Your VM's address 10.101.23.101 vCenter, step 0.1 Database login student_01 your student number with an underscore, not a hyphen, and not your email address Open in a browser tab Address vCenter https://vcenter0<N>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/ui Site A console https://console-openshift-console.apps.<A>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com Site B console https://console-openshift-console.apps.<B>.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com

docs.title: 0.1 Sign in to vCenter, and note your VM's address
docs.text:
1. Open the vCenter tab, choose Launch vSphere Client, then the SSO / Entra sign-in with your class account.
  2. Go to VMs and Templates → datacenter01 → vms → students → <your class ID> and select your VM, win-pg-s<NN> (for example student-03 → win-pg-s03).
  3. On its Summary tab, find IP Addresses. ✍️ Write it down: this is your VM's address (for example 10.101.23.103). You use it in step 0.4, and your VM keeps it after every move.

✅ Your VM is powered on, with three disks (60 GB, 5 GB and 10 GB).

docs.title: 0.2 Sign in to both OpenShift consoles
docs.text:
1. Open the site A console tab and choose Entra (SSO). Your vCenter sign-in carries over.
  2. Do the same in the site B console tab.
  3. In each, Home → Projects shows your own project, named your class ID (for example student-01-0024-012). You are admin there.

docs.title: 0.3 Open a command line
docs.text:
The command line is oc, signed in as you with a token you copy from the console:

  1. In the site A console, open your name (top right) → Copy login command → Display Token.
  2. Copy the line that starts with oc login --token=… --server=….

You can run it in either of two places.

docs.title: Option 1: oc on your own computer (outside this class)
docs.text: If your company allows it, install the oc client yourself: Getting started with the OpenShift CLI (the console's ? → Command Line Tools has the download). Installing it is outside this class's scope: the class needs only your browser. Paste the copied line into your terminal and press Enter.

docs.title: Option 2: a command line inside OpenShift (the class way)
docs.text:
Nothing to install. Use one of:

  • The console's Web Terminal: the >_ icon at the top right of the console opens a terminal already signed in as you. Click Start (leave the project as it is). It has oc; for your VM's database you use the one-line oc exec commands in 0.4.
  • Your class terminal: in your project, Workloads → Pods → sql-client-… → Terminal. It has oc and the class commands (dblogin, mark, sql, verify) ready, and already knows your VM's address and your database login. Sign its oc in: type oclogin and a space, paste the copied line, and press Enter.

⚠ Not the Windows VM's command prompt. Everything in this lab runs in one of the two terminals above.

📋 Copy and paste: paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V, ⌘V on a Mac); copy by selecting the text, then right-click → Copy. [verify: per browser]

docs.title: 0.4 Test: the cluster, then your VM's database
docs.text:
The cluster:

oc whoami            # your class ID, e.g. student-01-0024-012@lab-paragonmicro.com
oc get nodes         # the cluster's nodes, all Ready

Your VM's database, PostgreSQL inside your Windows VM, at your VM's address from 0.1 (the -h below). From oc anywhere (the Web Terminal, or your own computer), each step is one line: oc exec runs it inside your class terminal (sql-client).

⚠ Steps 1–4 are an example. Change two values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID (student-01 on booking 0024-012) your class ID, e.g. student-03-0024-012 (appears in every line, and twice in steps 2 and 4) 10.101.23.101 address of win-pg-s01, the Windows VM running the SQL server your VM's address, from vCenter in 0.1
  1. Sign in to the database, once (enter your class password):
oc exec -it -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- dblogin
  1. Inject a row: the class has started:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'start-class', 'Lab 0: signed in');"
  1. Read back every row you have posted, oldest first:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
  1. Prove them: no row lost, changed or reordered (one summary line, chain_ok = t):
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

💡 If a step says First sign in to your VM's database … dblogin, your class terminal restarted: do step 1 again.

✅ oc get nodes lists the nodes Ready, the read-back lists your start-class row, and verify shows chain_ok = t.

docs.title: Done
docs.text:
You are signed in to vCenter and both OpenShift clusters, you have a command line, and you reached your own VM's database. Go back to the Student Guide and continue with the next module, Demo 1.

Every demo uses the class commands for the same inject, read back and prove (mark, verify), plus load and alive: they are in the Toolkit, which each demo points to when you need it.

docs.title: Demo 1: VMware to OpenShift Virtualization (cold migration)
docs.text: Version 1.1.1 · draft · 2026-10-13 · class/demos/01-vmware-to-ove-cold.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
You move your own Windows Server + PostgreSQL VM off VMware vSphere and onto OpenShift Virtualization with the Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV). A cold migration copies the disks while the VM is off: simple and consistent, at the cost of an outage for the whole copy. Before and after the move you write a row into your VM's database and read every row back, so you can see your data survive the move.

Before you start: do Lab 0. You are signed in to the site A console, and your database rows from Lab 0 are there. Every command below runs in the console's Web Terminal (>_).

⚠ The commands are an example. Change these values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID and project (student-01 on booking 0024-012) your class ID win-pg-s01 your VM (s + your student number) your VM 10.101.23.101 your VM's address, the SQL server (it keeps it on OpenShift) your VM's address, from Lab 0.1 vcenter01 / VLAN 23 your booking's vCenter (N = 1) and VLAN (22 + N) from your instructor's N 🎬 Video: Demo 1: cold migration

🎬 Demo 1: cold migration: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 1.0 Inject: the demo has started
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'demo-started', 'Demo 1: cold migration');"

✅ It prints the row it wrote, with stage demo-started. (If it says First sign in … dblogin, run Lab 0's step 1 again.)

docs.title: 1.1 Check your migration plan, and the link to vCenter
docs.text:
The lab staged everything for you: a provider that links OpenShift to your vCenter, and your own migration plan, ready but not started.

Console (site A): Migration for Virtualization → Providers → ovedr-vcenter01.

✅ Status Ready, and Connected: OpenShift can log in to vCenter and read its inventory.

Console: Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → d1-win-pg-s01 (your plan is d1-<your VM>).

✅ Status Ready. Source provider ovedr-vcenter01, your VM, target project your class ID, type Cold. The network map puts your VM on your VLAN's bridge, so it keeps its address; the storage map puts its disks on ODF.

The same from the Web Terminal:

oc -n openshift-mtv get provider ovedr-vcenter01                     # READY True · CONNECTED True
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d1-win-pg-s01                           # READY True
My plan says "Cannot start" (critical concerns)

Two critical concerns block the start: the plan's maps don't cover your VM's network or its datastore. The two information concerns are fine for a cold migration.

Concern What it means Fix VMNetworksNotMapped (critical) Your VM's NIC is on a vSphere network (vm-network) that the plan's network map has no row for Map vm-network VMStorageNotMapped (critical) Your VM's disks are on a datastore (coresan01_data00) that the plan's storage map has no row for Map coresan01_data00 VM snapshot detected (info) Your VM has a snapshot. MTV migrates the VM's current state Nothing to do Disk serial numbers may be truncated (info) SCSI serials are shortened on OpenShift Nothing to do

Fix in the console: open the plan → Mappings tab → Edit mappings:

  1. Network: source vm-network → target your VLAN's bridge default/vmnet23 (keeps your address).
  2. Storage: source coresan01_data00 → target ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization.
  3. Save. The concerns clear within a minute, and the status changes from Cannot start to Ready.

docs.title: 1.2 Inject, then shut your VM down
docs.text:
Your database lives inside the VM, so write the "start" row before you shut it down:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'start-cold-migration', 'on vSphere');"

vCenter: VMs and Templates → datacenter01 → vms → students → student-01-0024-012 → win-pg-s01 → Actions → Power → Shut Down Guest OS. A clean guest shutdown flushes PostgreSQL to disk first.

✅ The VM shows Powered Off in vCenter.

docs.title: 1.3 Start the migration
docs.text:
Console (site A): Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → d1-win-pg-s01 → Start → confirm.

Watch it on the plan's page: expand your VM to see each step with a progress bar.

  1. Initialize and PreflightInspection
  2. DiskTransfer: three disks (C:, D: data, L: WAL), copied from vSphere
  3. ImageConversion: virt-v2v installs the virtio drivers and the QEMU guest agent, and removes VMware Tools
  4. VirtualMachineCreation
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d1-win-pg-s01 -w                        # Executing → Succeeded (Ctrl-C to stop watching)

✅ The plan shows Succeeded.

Or: create and start your own cold plan from the CLI (instead of the staged one)

This builds a cold plan like your staged d1-win-pg-s01, under a new name, so the staged plan stays as the lab built it. Use one of them: a VM can be in only one running plan. If you start this one, skip the console's Start above.

Set the values once. Every command below reads them:

# your class ID: MTV creates your VM in this project on site A
CLASS_ID=student-01-0024-012
# your VM's name in vCenter (MTV keeps the name on OpenShift)
VM=win-pg-s01
# the provider that links site A to your booking's vCenter ("ovedr-vcenter0" + N), and its maps
SRC=ovedr-vcenter01
# a NEW plan name, so this never touches the staged d1-win-pg-s01
PLAN=$CLASS_ID-cold-cli

Create the plan. The maps are the class's: -net-bridge keeps your VM on its VLAN (and its address), -storage puts its disks on ODF:

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: false
  targetNamespace: $CLASS_ID
  provider:
    source:      { name: $SRC, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: $SRC-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: $SRC-storage,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - name: $VM
EOF
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # READY True (Ctrl-C)

Start it: a Migration is what the console's Start button creates.

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN-run1, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOF
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # Executing → Succeeded (Ctrl-C)
A step failed: read the logs before you delete anything

A failed cold migration: ImageConversion (virt-v2v) failed, and the error says "See pod logs for details". There is no Cancel on a failed plan, only Delete, and deleting the plan deletes its pods and their logs, so read them first.

The conversion runs in a pod in your project, named after your plan. After a failure it stays there in status Error, with its full log.

Console: Workloads → Pods, project your class ID → the pod named after your plan → Logs.

Web Terminal:

oc -n student-01-0024-012 get pods | grep d1-win-pg-s01                                     # the conversion pod (Error)
POD=$(oc -n student-01-0024-012 get pods -o name | grep d1-win-pg-s01 | head -1)
oc -n student-01-0024-012 logs "$POD" | grep -E 'virt-v2v: error|error:|HTTP' | sort | uniq -c | tail

Read the log bottom up: the last virt-v2v: error: line is the verdict, and the lines above it are the cause. For example, HTTP 404 on a …-flat.vmdk URL means MTV could not read the VM's disk from vCenter. Show your instructor before you delete or archive the plan.

docs.title: 1.4 Review your VM on OpenShift, then power it on
docs.text:
Console (site A): Virtualization → VirtualMachines, project student-01-0024-012 → win-pg-s01.

Tab What you see Configuration → Network one NIC on default/vmnet23: your VLAN's bridge, the same VLAN the VM had on vSphere (port group vm-network, VLAN 23) Configuration → Storage three disks, now persistent volume claims on ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (ODF): 60 GB C:, 10 GB data, 5 GB WAL 
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vm win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{range .spec.template.spec.networks[*]}{.multus.networkName}{"\n"}{end}'   # default/vmnet23
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get pvc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SIZE:.spec.resources.requests.storage,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName

Power it on: Actions → Start. Wait for Running.

oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmi win-pg-s01 -w                      # Scheduling → Running (Ctrl-C to stop watching)

On the VM's Overview, the Guest agent shows as connected, and IP addresses shows 10.101.23.101: your VM kept its address, so your SQL server is still at the same -h as on vSphere.

✅ Running, guest agent connected, address 10.101.23.101.

docs.title: 1.5 Inject: the migration is complete, and read your rows back
docs.text:
Give Windows a minute to start PostgreSQL, then:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'cold-migration-complete', 'on OpenShift site A');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ The read-back lists, in order: start-class (Lab 0), demo-started, start-cold-migration (written on vSphere) and cold-migration-complete (written on OpenShift). ovedr_verify shows chain_ok = t: no row lost, changed or reordered by the move.

That is the end of Demo 1. Your VM now runs on OpenShift Virtualization, with every row it held on VMware.

docs.title: Bonus labs (optional)
docs.text:
1a to 1c start from your VM running on site A, where Demo 1 left it. 1d builds a new server next to it.

Bonus What you do Demo 1a: snapshot and restore snapshot your VM, destroy the database, bring it back from the snapshot's disks Demo 1b: live migration and storage migration move the running VM to another node, then move its disks to another storage class, with no reboot Demo 1c: cross-cluster migration link the two clusters in ACM, then move your VM from site A (ODF) to site B (NFS) Demo 1d: a cloud-native golden image build a new CentOS Stream 10 + PostgreSQL server purely in code, from Red Hat's boot source and a Template, and inject into it

Next: Demo 2: warm migration.

docs.title: Addendum: how the lab staged this demo, as code
docs.text:
Nothing you used in this demo was clicked together. The class's CI (the GitHub Actions workflow deploy.yml, action customize) declared every object, and it runs again on every booking with the same result: run it twice and the second run changes nothing. In order:

CI job Code What it declares mtv-install Ansible role mtv_operator checks MTV (installed by the OpenShift build, option ove: cnv-mtv), sets the pre-copy interval, grants students the right to create plans and migrations mtv-fabric automation/customize/mtv_fabric.sh the link to vCenter (a Secret + a Provider), and the NetworkMaps and StorageMap stage automation/customize/stage.sh one Plan per class VM, d1-<vm> (cold) and d2-<vm> (warm), not started migration-test automation/test/migrate_both.sh the proof: a test clone migrates from vSphere to each site with the same Plan + Migration you used, and its data is checked (action test-migration)

The chain MTV follows, and each object as the lab declares it (the Secret's password never appears in the code: CI reads it from the vault at run time):

# 1 · Provider: the link to vCenter. MTV reads its inventory (VMs, networks, datastores) through it.
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  type: vsphere
  url: https://vcenter01.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/sdk
  secret: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }   # user, password, the vCenter CA
---
# 2 · NetworkMap: vSphere port group → your VLAN's bridge on OpenShift, so the VM keeps its address
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: NetworkMap
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  provider: { source: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map:
    - { source: { name: vm-network }, destination: { type: multus, name: vmnet23, namespace: default } }
---
# 3 · StorageMap: vSphere datastore → OpenShift storage class (ODF on site A)
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageMap
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-storage, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  provider: { source: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map:
    - { source: { name: coresan01_data00 }, destination: { storageClass: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization } }
---
# 4 · Plan: which VM, to which project, through which maps. Staged, not started.
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: d1-win-pg-s01, namespace: openshift-mtv, labels: { ovedr/stage: plan, ovedr/type: cold } }
spec:
  warm: false
  targetNamespace: student-01-0024-012
  provider: { source: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map:
    network: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-storage,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms: [ { name: win-pg-s01 } ]

5 · Migration: the only object left to you. The console's Start creates it, as does the CLI box in 1.3.

Read the live ones from your Web Terminal:

oc -n openshift-mtv get provider ovedr-vcenter01 -o yaml
oc -n openshift-mtv get networkmap ovedr-vcenter01-net-bridge -o yaml
oc -n openshift-mtv get storagemap ovedr-vcenter01-storage -o yaml
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d1-win-pg-s01 -o yaml

Field by field, with the console screens for each: Lab S §S.5–S.8 and §S.12.

docs.title: Demo 1a: snapshot and restore (bonus)
docs.text: Version 1.0.0 · draft · 2026-10-13 · class/demos/01a-snapshot-restore.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
You take a snapshot of your running VM, destroy its database for real, then bring the data back by attaching the snapshot's disks. The rows you read back show the recovery point: everything written before the snapshot returns, and what you wrote after it does not.

Before you start: finish Demo 1. Your VM runs on site A, and every command runs in the site A console's Web Terminal (>_). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → your VM → Console, then log in as .\student-01 (your Windows login).

⚠ The commands are an example for student-01-0024-012, VM win-pg-s01 at 10.101.23.101. Change them to your class ID, your VM and its address before you run them.

⚠️ Data and WAL go together. PostgreSQL keeps its data on D: and its write-ahead log on L:. If you restore only D: and keep today's L:, PostgreSQL replays the newer WAL on start, including the DROP DATABASE, and you lose the database again. Restore both disks from the same snapshot. A VM snapshot with the guest agent freezes all disks at the same instant, so its D: and L: match.

🎬 Video: Demo 1a: snapshot and restore

🎬 Demo 1a: snapshot and restore: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 1a.1 Inject, then snapshot
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'before-snapshot', 'this row must come back');"

Console: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → win-pg-s01 → Snapshots → Take snapshot, name it win-pg-s01-snap. Or from the Web Terminal:

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata: { name: win-pg-s01-snap, namespace: student-01-0024-012 }
spec:
  source: { apiGroup: kubevirt.io, kind: VirtualMachine, name: win-pg-s01 }
EOF
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmsnapshot win-pg-s01-snap -w            # Ctrl-C when READYTOUSE is true

✅ The snapshot is Ready, with indications Online and GuestAgent: taken while running, with the disks frozen together.

Now write a row after the snapshot. It exists only in the live database, so the restore must lose it:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'after-snapshot', 'this row must NOT come back');"

docs.title: 1a.2 Destroy the database
docs.text:
In your VM's console, in an elevated PowerShell (Run as administrator), stop the heartbeat writer so that it doesn't recreate anything:

Disable-ScheduledTask -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat | Out-Null
Stop-ScheduledTask    -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat

Then drop the database. The bcdr role owns it, and its password is the instructor's, so 🧑‍🏫 ask your instructor to run this with your VM's address:

# 🧑‍🏫 instructor, in their Web Terminal: the class pod in ovedr-app holds the bcdr owner's password
oc -n ovedr-app exec -i deploy/sql-client -- psql -h 10.101.23.101 -U bcdr -d postgres -c 'DROP DATABASE bcdr WITH (FORCE);'

Confirm the damage:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"

✅ FATAL: database "bcdr" does not exist. That is the disaster.

docs.title: 1a.3 Take the damaged disks offline
docs.text:
In the VM's elevated PowerShell:

Stop-Service postgresql-16
$bad = foreach ($l in 'D','L') { Get-Partition -DriveLetter $l | Get-Disk }
$bad | Format-Table Number, FriendlyName, SerialNumber, @{n='GB';e={[math]::Round($_.Size/1GB)}}
foreach ($l in 'D','L') { Get-Partition -DriveLetter $l | Remove-PartitionAccessPath -AccessPath "$($l):\" }
$bad | ForEach-Object { Set-Disk -Number $_.Number -IsOffline $true }

docs.title: 1a.4 Create volumes from the snapshot's D: and L:, and hot-plug them
docs.text:
Set the values once. Every command in this step reads them:

# your class ID: the project your VM, its disks and the snapshot live in
CLASS_ID=student-01-0024-012
# your VM, and the snapshot you took in 1a.1
VM=win-pg-s01
SNAP=$VM-snap

The snapshot holds one VolumeSnapshot per disk. List them, and note the 10Gi (D:, data) and 5Gi (L:, WAL) rows:

CONTENT=$(oc -n $CLASS_ID get vmsnapshot $SNAP -o jsonpath='{.status.virtualMachineSnapshotContentName}')
oc -n $CLASS_ID get vmsnapshotcontent "$CONTENT" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.volumeBackups[*]}{.persistentVolumeClaim.metadata.name}{"  "}{.persistentVolumeClaim.spec.resources.requests.storage}{"  "}{.volumeSnapshotName}{"\n"}{end}'

Copy four names from that list:

# the 10Gi row: your data disk (D:) and its VolumeSnapshot
DATA_PVC='<10Gi pvc>'
DATA_SNAP='<its volumesnapshot>'
# the 5Gi row: your WAL disk (L:) and its VolumeSnapshot, from the SAME snapshot so data and WAL match
WAL_PVC='<5Gi pvc>'
WAL_SNAP='<its volumesnapshot>'

Create a volume from each VolumeSnapshot, with the same class, mode and size as the original:

restore_pvc() {   # restore_pvc <original pvc> <volumesnapshot> <new name>
  oc -n $CLASS_ID get pvc "$1" -o json | jq --arg s "$2" --arg n "$3" '{
    apiVersion: "v1", kind: "PersistentVolumeClaim",
    metadata: {name: $n, namespace: .metadata.namespace},
    spec: {storageClassName: .spec.storageClassName, accessModes: .spec.accessModes,
           volumeMode: .spec.volumeMode, resources: .spec.resources,
           dataSource: {apiGroup: "snapshot.storage.k8s.io", kind: "VolumeSnapshot", name: $s}}}' | oc apply -f -
}
restore_pvc "$DATA_PVC" "$DATA_SNAP" $VM-restored-data
restore_pvc "$WAL_PVC"  "$WAL_SNAP"  $VM-restored-wal
oc -n $CLASS_ID get pvc $VM-restored-data $VM-restored-wal -w     # Bound (Ctrl-C)

Hot-plug both into the running VM. The serial (data, wal) is how Windows will tell them apart:

virtctl -n $CLASS_ID addvolume $VM --volume-name=$VM-restored-data --serial=data --persist
virtctl -n $CLASS_ID addvolume $VM --volume-name=$VM-restored-wal  --serial=wal  --persist
oc -n $CLASS_ID get vmi $VM -o jsonpath='{range .status.volumeStatus[*]}{.name}{"  "}{.phase}{"\n"}{end}'

✅ Both restored volumes show Ready [verify: hot-plug on this cluster, and the vioscsi driver in the guest].

docs.title: 1a.5 Bring the restored disks online as D: and L:, start PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Update-HostStorageCache
foreach ($m in @(@{Serial='data'; Letter='D'}, @{Serial='wal'; Letter='L'})) {
  $d = Get-Disk | Where-Object { $_.SerialNumber -eq $m.Serial }
  Set-Disk -Number $d.Number -IsOffline   $false
  Set-Disk -Number $d.Number -IsReadOnly  $false
  Get-Partition -DiskNumber $d.Number | Where-Object Type -eq 'Basic' | Set-Partition -NewDriveLetter $m.Letter
}
Get-Volume -DriveLetter D, L | Format-Table DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, Size, HealthStatus
Start-Service postgresql-16
Enable-ScheduledTask -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat | Out-Null
Start-ScheduledTask  -TaskName bcdr-heartbeat

(The restored disks are copies of the originals, so Windows may first report a signature collision. Bringing the copy online while the originals are offline gives it a new signature. That is expected.)

docs.title: 1a.6 Inject, and read back what came back
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'snapshot-restored', 'database back from the snapshot');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ The database exists again and chain_ok = t. The read-back runs start-class … cold-migration-complete, before-snapshot, then snapshot-restored. ✅ after-snapshot is gone. It was written after the snapshot, so it was never in it. That is the recovery point: a restore returns you to the moment of the snapshot, not to the moment of the disaster.

docs.title: The other way: restore the whole VM
docs.text:
Swapping disks by hand shows what a restore really is. In production you would restore the whole VM in one step, at the cost of a restart: VM → Snapshots → win-pg-s01-snap → Restore. Or:

virtctl -n student-01-0024-012 stop win-pg-s01
oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineRestore
metadata: { name: win-pg-s01-restore, namespace: student-01-0024-012 }
spec:
  target: { apiGroup: kubevirt.io, kind: VirtualMachine, name: win-pg-s01 }
  virtualMachineSnapshotName: win-pg-s01-snap
EOF
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmrestore win-pg-s01-restore -w          # COMPLETE true (Ctrl-C)
virtctl -n student-01-0024-012 start win-pg-s01

Tidy up: after the disk swap, your VM carries two extra disks and its original D: and L: are offline. Before the next demo, either restore the whole VM (above), or stop the VM and remove the old volumes in Configuration → Storage [verify: BL-D11, a clean "post-bonus" state for demos 2-4].

Back to: Demo 1 · Next: Demo 2: warm migration.

docs.title: Demo 1b: live migration and storage migration (bonus)
docs.text: Version 1.0.0 · draft · 2026-10-13 · class/demos/01b-live-and-storage-migration.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
Two moves on a running VM, with no reboot: a live migration moves its memory and CPU to another node, and a storage migration moves one of its disks to another storage class (ODF → NFS) while Windows and PostgreSQL keep running. You write a row before and after each move and read them back.

Before you start: finish Demo 1. Your VM runs on site A, and every command runs in the site A console's Web Terminal (>_).

⚠ The commands are an example for student-01-0024-012, VM win-pg-s01 at 10.101.23.101. Change them to your class ID, your VM and its address before you run them.

🎬 Video: Demo 1b: live migration and storage migration

🎬 Demo 1b: live migration and storage migration: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 1b.1 Inject, and check the VM can live-migrate
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'before-live-migration', 'running on one node');"
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmi win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{.status.nodeName}  LiveMigratable={.status.conditions[?(@.type=="LiveMigratable")].status}{"\n"}'

✅ LiveMigratable=True. ✍️ Note the node it runs on now. A live migration needs the disks reachable from both nodes at once (ReadWriteMany): ODF's ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization is. If it says False, the condition's message names the reason, usually a mounted CD.

docs.title: 1b.2 Live-migrate to another node
docs.text:
Console: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → win-pg-s01 → Actions → Migrate → Compute. Or:

virtctl -n student-01-0024-012 migrate win-pg-s01
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmim -w                                 # … Succeeded (Ctrl-C)
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmi win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{.status.nodeName}{"\n"}'

✅ The VM runs on a different node, and it never stopped: the console's VM Overview shows the new node and no restart.

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'after-live-migration', 'running on another node');"

docs.title: 1b.3 Storage migration: move the data disk from ODF to NFS, while it runs [verify]
docs.text:
Your VM's disks are on ODF (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization). Move the 10 GB data disk (D:) to nfs-csi, with the VM running. OpenShift Virtualization copies the disk in the background, then switches the VM to the new copy with a live migration.

[verify: storage live migration on OpenShift Virtualization 4.19 (spec.updateVolumesStrategy: Migration, vmRolloutStrategy: LiveUpdate is set on this cluster); ODF block → NFS filesystem; whether the console's Actions → Migrate → Storage offers the same]

Find the data disk's volume (the 10Gi one):

oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vm win-pg-s01 -o json | jq -r '.spec.template.spec.volumes[] | "\(.name)  \(.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName // .dataVolume.name)"'
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get pvc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SIZE:.spec.resources.requests.storage,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName

Set the one value this step needs, from the list above:

# the data disk's current volume (the 10Gi one on ODF): the disk you are moving
OLD='<the 10Gi pvc from the list above>'

Create an empty 10Gi target volume on nfs-csi:

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: cdi.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: DataVolume
metadata: { name: win-pg-s01-data-nfs, namespace: student-01-0024-012 }
spec:
  source: { blank: {} }
  storage:
    storageClassName: nfs-csi
    accessModes: [ ReadWriteMany ]
    resources: { requests: { storage: 10Gi } }
EOF
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get dv win-pg-s01-data-nfs -w                # Succeeded (Ctrl-C)

Point the VM's data disk at the new volume, and tell it to migrate the data (not just swap the disk):

oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vm win-pg-s01 -o json | jq --arg old "$OLD" '
  .spec.updateVolumesStrategy = "Migration"
  | .spec.template.spec.volumes |= map(
      if ((.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName // .dataVolume.name) == $old)
      then {name: .name, dataVolume: {name: "win-pg-s01-data-nfs"}} else . end)' | oc replace -f -
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmim -w                                 # a migration runs and Succeeds (Ctrl-C)
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmi win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{range .status.volumeStatus[*]}{.name}  {.persistentVolumeClaimInfo.claimName}{"\n"}{end}'

✅ The data disk now reads win-pg-s01-data-nfs (nfs-csi), and the VM never restarted. In the console: VM → Configuration → Storage shows the data disk on nfs-csi.

docs.title: 1b.4 Inject, and read back
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'after-storage-migration', 'data disk on NFS');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ After Demo 1's rows: before-live-migration, after-live-migration and after-storage-migration, in order, with chain_ok = t. PostgreSQL kept running through both moves, so nothing between them is missing.

docs.title: Demo 1c: cross-cluster migration, site A to site B (bonus)
docs.text: Version 1.0.0 · draft · 2026-10-13 · class/demos/01c-ocp-vm-cross-cluster-migration.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
Your VM already runs on OpenShift: Demo 1 (cold) or Demo 2 (warm) moved it off VMware onto site A. Now you move it to a second OpenShift cluster, site B. Advanced Cluster Management (ACM) links the two clusters into one fleet, and MTV moves the VM between them. The two sites use different storage, so the move is also a storage migration: site A's disks on ODF are copied onto site B's NFS. As in every demo, you write a row before and after the move and read them all back.

Before you start: your VM runs on site A (after Demo 1 or 2). You are signed in to both consoles. Commands run in each console's Web Terminal (>_); each step says which site.

⚠ The commands are an example. Change these values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID and project, the same on both sites your class ID win-pg-s01 your VM your VM 10.101.23.101 your VM's address, the SQL server: it keeps it on site B too your VM's address ocp-lz1 → ocp-lz2 site A → site B (provider ovedr-ocp-lz1, on site B) your booking's A and B 🎬 Video: Demo 1c: cross-cluster migration

🎬 Demo 1c: cross-cluster migration: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 1c.0 Inject: the demo has started (site A)
docs.text: oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'cross-cluster-started', 'Demo 1c: running on site A');"

docs.title: 1c.1 ACM: the two clusters, linked (site B)
docs.text:
Site B runs the ACM hub, and site A is imported into it as a managed cluster.

Console (site B): switch the perspective at the top left to All Clusters → Infrastructure → Clusters.

✅ ocp-lz1 (site A) shows Ready, next to local-cluster (site B itself).

oc get managedclusters                              # ocp-lz1  JOINED True  AVAILABLE True

Your VM, seen from the hub: All Clusters → Infrastructure → Virtual machines [verify: ACM 2.13 fleet virtualization view on the hub]. win-pg-s01 shows on cluster ocp-lz1, in your project, Running.

ACM shows you where the VM is; MTV does the move.

docs.title: 1c.2 MTV: the link to site A, and the maps (site B)
docs.text:
Console (site B): Migration for Virtualization → Providers → ovedr-ocp-lz1.

✅ Ready and Connected: site B's MTV reads site A's VMs.

Map (on site B) What it does for your VM Network map ovedr-ocp-lz1-net default/vmnet23 on site A → default/vmnet23 on site B: same VLAN, so your VM keeps its address Storage map ovedr-ocp-lz1-storage ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (ODF, site A) → nfs-csi (NFS, site B): the storage migration 
oc -n openshift-mtv get provider ovedr-ocp-lz1                                     # READY True · CONNECTED True
oc -n openshift-mtv get storagemap ovedr-ocp-lz1-storage -o jsonpath='{.spec.map}{"\n"}'   # ODF → nfs-csi

MTV doesn't move the disks themselves: for each one it creates a new volume on site B in nfs-csi and fills it by reading the disk on site A over the network. Site A's disks are left untouched.

docs.title: 1c.3 Inject, then stop your VM (site A)
docs.text:
Write the "start" row before the VM stops, while its database still answers:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'start-cross-cluster-migration', 'last row on site A');"

Console (site A): Virtualization → VirtualMachines → win-pg-s01 → Actions → Stop.

✅ The VM shows Stopped.

docs.title: 1c.4 Create your plan, and start it (site B)
docs.text:
This plan isn't staged: you create it, then start it.

Console (site B): Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → Create plan:

Field Value Plan name d1c-win-pg-s01 (d1c-<your VM>) Plan project openshift-mtv Source provider ovedr-ocp-lz1 Target provider host (site B) Target project student-01-0024-012 Virtual machines only your VM, win-pg-s01 (in project student-01-0024-012) Network map ovedr-ocp-lz1-net (use the existing map) Storage map ovedr-ocp-lz1-storage (use the existing map) Migration type Cold

Create plan. When it shows Ready, click Start → confirm. Expand your VM on the plan's page to watch DiskTransfer: three disks copied from ODF on site A into nfs-csi on site B.

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d1c-win-pg-s01 -w      # Ready → Executing → Succeeded (Ctrl-C)
Or: create and start the plan from the CLI (site B Web Terminal)

This builds the same plan under its own name, d1c-cli-win-pg-s01, so it never touches one you made in the console. Use one of them: a VM can be in only one running plan.

Set the values once. Every command below reads them:

# your class ID: your project on both sites, and where MTV creates the VM on site B
CLASS_ID=student-01-0024-012
# your VM's name on site A (MTV keeps the name on site B)
VM=win-pg-s01
# the provider on site B that reads site A ("ovedr-ocp-" + site A's slot), and its two maps
SRC=ovedr-ocp-lz1
# a NEW plan name, so this never overwrites a plan you created in the console
PLAN=d1c-cli-$VM

Create the plan:

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: false
  targetNamespace: $CLASS_ID
  provider:
    source:      { name: $SRC, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: $SRC-net,     namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: $SRC-storage, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - { name: $VM, namespace: $CLASS_ID }
EOF
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # READY True (Ctrl-C)

Start it: a Migration is what the console's Start button creates.

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN-run1, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOF
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # Executing → Succeeded (Ctrl-C)

If the plan reports a critical condition, read it before you start: usually a network or storage class on site A that the maps don't cover.

✅ The plan shows Succeeded.

docs.title: 1c.5 Review your VM on site B, then power it on (site B)
docs.text:
Console (site B): Virtualization → VirtualMachines, project student-01-0024-012 → win-pg-s01.

Tab What you see Configuration → Network the NIC on default/vmnet23: the same VLAN as on site A Configuration → Storage three disks, now on nfs-csi (they were on ODF on site A): the storage migration 
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get pvc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SIZE:.spec.resources.requests.storage,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName

If it isn't running yet: Actions → Start, and wait for Running. On its Overview, IP addresses shows 10.101.23.101: the same address on a different cluster.

✅ Running on site B, disks on nfs-csi, address 10.101.23.101.

💡 The source is stopped, not deleted. Site A still holds your VM, stopped, as of start-cross-cluster-migration. Never run both copies at once: they share an address and a database identity. To roll back, stop it on site B and start it on site A (rows written on B are not on A). Once you've checked site B, your instructor can delete the site A copy.

docs.title: 1c.6 Inject: the move is complete, and read your rows back (site B)
docs.text:
Site B has its own class terminal (sql-client, in your project), which needs its own database sign-in once:

oc exec -it -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- dblogin

Give Windows a minute to start PostgreSQL, then:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'cross-cluster-migration-complete', 'running on site B, disks on NFS');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ Every row from Lab 0 and Demo 1 (or 2) is there, then cross-cluster-started, start-cross-cluster-migration (both written on site A) and cross-cluster-migration-complete (written on site B), in order, with chain_ok = t.

That is the end of Demo 1c. Your VM crossed from one OpenShift cluster to another, and from ODF to NFS, with every row it held.

docs.title: Demo 1d: a cloud-native golden image (bonus)
docs.text: Version 1.0.0 · draft · 2026-10-13 · class/demos/01d-vm-cloudnative-golden-image.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
In Demo 1 you moved an existing Windows VM: a pet, built once by hand in vCenter, patched in place, and copied whenever someone needs another. Here you build its replacement from scratch, in code: a CentOS Stream 10 server running the same PostgreSQL database, with its own logins, its data and its WAL (the log) on separate disks, and its services running. Nothing is installed by hand and nothing is baked into an image:

The pet golden image (vSphere) The cloud-native golden image (OpenShift) Base OS an ISO you install, then keep patching yourself Red Hat's boot source, a cloud image that OpenShift Virtualization keeps up to date Customization clicks and scripts inside the image, then sysprep and Convert to Template a Template with cloud-init: text in git, reviewed like code A new server clone the template, then fix what drifted the same code, every time: identical servers in minutes Proof it works someone checks by hand CI deploys it on every lab build and tests it with SQL

You deploy it twice over: in the console (as in the video), and with one command. Then you inject rows into the new Linux PostgreSQL and read them back, exactly as you did on Windows.

Before you start: do Lab 0. You are signed in to the site A console, and your class terminal is signed in to the database (dblogin, once). Your Windows VM can be anywhere: this demo builds a new VM next to it. Commands run in the console's Web Terminal (>_).

⚠ The commands are an example. Change these values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID and project your class ID pg-s01-centos10 the new VM's name pg-s<NN>-centos10 10.101.23.151 the new VM's address: VLAN 23, 150 + your student number 10.101.<22 + N>.<150 + NN> 23 your booking's VLAN (22 + N, vcenter01 → 23) from your instructor's N student-01 / student_01 your Linux login / your database login (underscore) yours 🎬 Video: Demo 1d: a cloud-native golden image

🎬 Demo 1d: a cloud-native golden image: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 1d.1 Look at the golden image: it's code
docs.text:
The lab published the customer's Template, ovedr-centos10-postgres, on both clusters.

Console (site A): Virtualization → Catalog → Template catalog. Find CentOS Stream 10 + PostgreSQL 16 (class) (filter on PostgreSQL; it is a user template, not a Red Hat one) [verify]. Open it: the boot source is Red Hat's CentOS Stream 10, with three disks and your VLAN's network.

The same from the Web Terminal: what it asks for, and the code itself:

oc process --parameters -n openshift ovedr-centos10-postgres
oc get template -n openshift ovedr-centos10-postgres -o yaml | less          # q to quit
In the Template What it does dataVolumeTemplates the system disk, cloned from Red Hat's centos-stream10 boot source, plus two empty disks: 10 GB for the data, 5 GB for the WAL networks one NIC on your VLAN's bridge (default/vmnet23), so the server has its own address on the lab network cloudInitNoCloud.networkData that address, its gateway and the lab's DNS cloudInitNoCloud.userData cloud-init, run on first boot: formats and mounts the two disks, installs PostgreSQL 16 with its WAL on its own disk, loads the class's marks toolkit, creates your Linux and database logins, starts the database and a heartbeat

The whole file is also on the class site: ovedr-centos10-postgres.yaml.

docs.title: 1d.2 Deploy it
docs.text:
Do one of the two. Both create the same VM.

Console (site A), as in the video: in the Template catalog, open CentOS Stream 10 + PostgreSQL 16 (class) → Customize VirtualMachine → project student-01-0024-012, and fill in the parameters:

Parameter Example VM name pg-s01-centos10 VLAN 23 IP address 10.101.23.151 Linux login student-01 Database login student_01 Password (Linux and database) your class password

Then Create VirtualMachine.

Or, the Web Terminal: the whole server is one command. It asks for your password, so it never appears on screen:

read -rsp 'Your class password: ' PW; echo; oc process -n openshift ovedr-centos10-postgres -p NAME=pg-s01-centos10 -p VLAN=23 -p IP=10.101.23.151 -p OS_USER=student-01 -p DB_USER=student_01 -p DB_PASSWORD="$PW" | oc apply -n student-01-0024-012 -f -; unset PW

✅ virtualmachine.kubevirt.io/pg-s01-centos10 created.

💡 Your password is in the VM's cloud-init, readable by you and the instructors in your project. That is fine for a lab account that dies with the booking. In production, cloud-init comes from a Secret (cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef), so the VM's definition holds no password.

docs.title: 1d.3 Watch it build itself
docs.text:
Console: Virtualization → VirtualMachines → pg-s01-centos10. It goes Provisioning (the disks are created: the system disk is cloned from the boot source), Starting, then Running.

oc -n student-01-0024-012 get dv                                     # pg-s01-centos10, -pgdata, -pgwal: Succeeded
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmi pg-s01-centos10 -w                 # Running (Ctrl-C to stop watching)

Once it is Running, cloud-init installs and configures PostgreSQL: allow a few minutes. Open the VM's Console tab and log in as student-01 with your class password, then:

cloud-init status --wait                                 # status: done
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINT                      # vdc pgdata /var/lib/pgsql/data · vdd pgwal /var/lib/pgsql/wal
systemctl is-active postgresql ovedr-heartbeat           # active, active
sudo ls -l /var/lib/pgsql/data/pg_wal                    # → /var/lib/pgsql/wal/pg_wal: the WAL on its own disk

✅ cloud-init done, both database disks mounted, both services active. Every one of these was declared in the Template, and none was typed by hand.

docs.title: 1d.4 Inject into your new Linux PostgreSQL, and read it back
docs.text:
Same commands as on Windows, at the new address. Your class terminal's dblogin works here too: same login, same password, a different server.

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.151 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'cloudnative-started', 'Demo 1d: CentOS Stream 10 from the Template');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.151 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_load('student-01-0024-012', 'cloudnative-load', 100);"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.151 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.151 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ The read-back starts fresh at cloudnative-started, then your 100 cloudnative-load rows, and ovedr_verify shows chain_ok = t. A new server has a new database: your Windows VM's rows are still on your Windows VM.

Is it alive, and what is it?

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.151 -c "SELECT count(*) AS beats, date_trunc('second', clock_timestamp() - max(ts)) AS staleness FROM heartbeat;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.151 -x -c "SELECT version(); SELECT platform, qemu_ga, virtio FROM guest_tools ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1;"

✅ staleness under 10 seconds, PostgreSQL 16 on Linux, platform kvm, QEMU guest agent active, virtio drivers: the same checks as your migrated Windows VM, on a server that was never migrated.

docs.title: 1d.5 Rebuild it: the point of a golden image as code
docs.text:
A pet is repaired. Cattle are replaced. Delete the server and deploy it again from the same Template:

oc -n student-01-0024-012 delete vm pg-s01-centos10                  # the VM and its three disks

Then run 1d.2 again. In a few minutes you have the same server at the same address, with an empty marks table: every setting came from code, so nothing drifted and nothing was forgotten.

That is the end of Demo 1d. You built a database server purely in code, from Red Hat's maintained image, and proved it with your own rows.

💡 One copy at a time on an address. Delete or stop your pg-s01-centos10 when you're done: its address is yours alone.

docs.title: Addendum: how the lab staged this demo, as code
docs.text:
CI job Code What it does golden-linux automation/customize/golden_linux.sh builds the Template and applies it to namespace openshift on every site that has the CentOS Stream 10 boot source (same job) the proof deploys a test VM from the Template (ovedr-ci-centos10, 10.101.<VLAN>.98), waits for PostgreSQL, writes a mark, checks chain_ok, the heartbeat and the guest tools, then deletes the VM. The run's summary shows how long the server took to answer (build) automation/tools/centos10_template.sh assembles the Template from one cloud-init file (workload/centos10/user-data.yaml) and the class's SQL (workload/sql/), the same schema and toolkit the Windows VMs run. A test fails if the published copy differs from what it builds

The customer's version of this is a short pipeline: change the cloud-init in git → CI builds the Template, deploys a test VM, runs its checks → the Template is published for everyone. The base OS comes from Red Hat's boot source, which OpenShift Virtualization updates on its own; your code stays the same.

docs.title: Demo 2: VMware to OpenShift Virtualization (warm migration)
docs.text:
Version 2.2.0 · draft · 2026-10-14 · class/demos/02-vmware-to-ove-warm.md

⚠ Status, 2026-10-14: this demo can't run for now. VDDK is no longer available to us.

A warm migration needs the VMware Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK): MTV uses it to read the blocks that changed while the VM runs (vSphere's Changed Block Tracking). VDDK has been pulled, and Red Hat has no generally available warm migration path from vSphere without it: a VDDK-independent transfer is in Developer Preview only (see Without VDDK: the paths Red Hat offers). So the staged warm plan d2-<your VM> stops at VDDKInitImageUnavailable (2.1) and never completes.

What still works: the cold migration in Demo 1. Without VDDK, MTV reads the disks over vCenter/ESXi HTTPS instead; it is slower, and the VM is down for its whole disk copy instead of a cutover of a few minutes. The "move from VMware with near-zero downtime" story becomes "a scheduled cold migration".

In class: do Demo 1 and its bonus labs, then Demo 1c, 1d and 4. Read this guide to learn how warm migration works; the steps below stay as they are for when VDDK, or a supported path without it, is available again.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
You move your Windows Server + PostgreSQL VM off VMware vSphere and onto OpenShift Virtualization again, this time warm. A warm migration copies the disks while the VM keeps running: a first full copy, then every 5 minutes only the blocks that changed. The VM stops only for the cutover, a last small copy, so the outage is minutes instead of the whole copy. vSphere's Changed Block Tracking (CBT) is what tells MTV which blocks changed, so you turn it on first. You write rows before, during and after the move, read them all back, and measure the real outage from your VM's own heartbeat.

Phase Your VM What MTV does Pre-copy 1 running snapshots each disk on vSphere and copies the whole disk Pre-copy 2, 3, … running every 5 minutes, copies only the blocks changed since the last round (CBT) Cutover stopped one last snapshot, copies the last small change, converts the drivers, starts the VM on OpenShift

Before you start: do Lab 0. You are signed in to the site A console. Every command below runs in the console's Web Terminal (>_). Your VM must be running on vSphere:

  • Straight after Lab 0: it is. Go to 2.0.
  • After Demo 1: your VM runs on OpenShift and the vSphere original is powered off. Both use the same address, so only one may run at a time. Stop the OpenShift copy first (Virtualization → VirtualMachines → win-pg-s01 → Actions → Stop), then power the original on in vCenter (win-pg-s01 → Actions → Power → Power On). The original holds your rows up to start-cold-migration. cold-migration-complete was written on the OpenShift copy, so the original doesn't have it, and that's expected.

⚠ The commands are an example. Change these values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID and project (student-01 on booking 0024-012) your class ID win-pg-s01 your VM (s + your student number); on OpenShift it lands as win-pg-s01-warm your VM 10.101.23.101 your VM's address, the SQL server (it keeps it on OpenShift) your VM's address, from Lab 0.1 vcenter01 / VLAN 23 your booking's vCenter (N = 1) and VLAN (22 + N) from your instructor's N 🎬 Video: Demo 2: warm migration

🎬 Demo 2: warm migration: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 2.0 Inject: the demo has started
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'demo-started', 'Demo 2: warm migration');"

✅ It prints the row it wrote, with stage demo-started. (If it says First sign in … dblogin, run Lab 0's step 1 again. If it can't connect, your VM isn't running on vSphere yet: see Before you start.)

docs.title: 2.1 Check the link to vCenter, and your warm plan
docs.text:
The lab staged a warm plan for you, ready but not started: d2-win-pg-s01 (d2-<your VM>). It lands your VM on site A as win-pg-s01-warm, so it never collides with a Demo 1 copy.

Console (site A): Migration for Virtualization → Providers → ovedr-vcenter01.

✅ Status Ready, and Connected.

Console: Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → d2-win-pg-s01.

✅ Type Warm, source provider ovedr-vcenter01, your VM, target project your class ID. The status is not Ready yet: expand your VM to see why.

Concern What it means Who fixes it VMMissingChangedBlockTracking your VM's disks don't have CBT on, so MTV can't copy only the changes you, in 2.2 VDDKInitImageUnavailable the provider has no VDDK image, the VMware library MTV needs to read changed blocks expected for now: VDDK is unavailable (see the status note at the top). Stop here

The same from the Web Terminal:

oc -n openshift-mtv get provider ovedr-vcenter01 -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}  vddk={.spec.settings.vddkInitImage}{"\n"}'   # Ready  vddk=<an image>
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}{"\n"}{end}'

✅ The provider shows a vddk= image, and the plan's only concern is VMMissingChangedBlockTracking.

docs.title: 2.2 Turn on Changed Block Tracking
docs.text:
CBT is one switch for the VM (ctkEnabled) plus one for each disk (scsi0:N.ctkEnabled). vCenter accepts them only while the VM is off, and they take effect at the next power-on.

Shut it down. vCenter: VMs and Templates → datacenter01 → vms → students → student-01-0024-012 → win-pg-s01 → Actions → Power → Shut Down Guest OS. Wait for Powered Off.

Add the four parameters. win-pg-s01 → Edit Settings → Advanced Parameters. For each row, type the Attribute and Value, then click ADD:

Attribute Value ctkEnabled true scsi0:0.ctkEnabled true scsi0:1.ctkEnabled true scsi0:2.ctkEnabled true

Adding a row: Attribute ctkEnabled, Value true, then ADD. The filter (funnel icon) set to ctk shows only the CBT rows.

All four rows set: the VM, plus scsi0:0, scsi0:1 and scsi0:2 for its three disks. Click OK.

Check your disks really are scsi0:0, 0:1 and 0:2

Edit Settings → Virtual Hardware: expand each Hard disk and read its Virtual Device Node, for example SCSI controller 0 : SCSI(0:1). The class VMs have three disks on one controller: 60 GB C:, 5 GB L: (WAL) and 10 GB D: (data). If a node differs, use its number in the parameter name.

Power it back on: Actions → Power → Power On.

✅ Within a minute or two the plan d2-win-pg-s01 shows Ready, and the CBT concern is gone:

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}{"\n"}{end}'   # Ready=True

If the concern stays, a disk is missing its scsi0:N.ctkEnabled, or the VM hasn't been powered on since you set it.

Give Windows a minute to start PostgreSQL, then check that the shutdown lost nothing:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ chain_ok = t.

docs.title: 2.3 Start the warm migration, and keep writing
docs.text:
Console (site A): Migration for Virtualization → Migration plans → d2-win-pg-s01 → Start → confirm.

Your VM keeps running on vSphere. Expand it on the plan's page: MTV takes a snapshot on vSphere and copies the whole of each disk (the first pre-copy). After that, every 5 minutes it copies only what changed. In vCenter, your VM's Snapshots show MTV's snapshot for each round.

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -w                        # EXECUTING True (Ctrl-C to stop watching)

Give it something to copy. The database is busy while it copies: write a burst of 500 rows now, and again after each pre-copy round if you like:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_load('student-01-0024-012', 'warm-precopy-load', 500);"

✅ It prints rows_written = 500. Your VM is still serving its database in the middle of the migration.

Count the pre-copies:

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='pre-copies done: {.status.migration.vms[0].warm.successes}  next: {.status.migration.vms[0].warm.nextPrecopyAt}{"\n"}'

✅ Wait for at least two pre-copies. The first carries the whole disks; later ones carry only the changed blocks, so they're much quicker. That difference is CBT at work.

Or: create and start your own warm plan from the CLI (instead of the staged one)

This builds a warm plan like your staged d2-win-pg-s01, under a new name, so the staged plan stays as the lab built it. Use one of them: a VM can be in only one running plan. If you start this one, skip the console's Start above, and cut over with the last command below instead of the console.

Set the values once. Every command below reads them:

# your class ID: MTV creates your VM in this project on site A
CLASS_ID=student-01-0024-012
# your VM's name in vCenter
VM=win-pg-s01
# the provider that links site A to your booking's vCenter ("ovedr-vcenter0" + N), and its maps
SRC=ovedr-vcenter01
# a NEW plan name, so this never touches the staged d2-win-pg-s01
PLAN=$CLASS_ID-warm-cli

Create the plan. warm: true is the only difference from a cold plan; targetName gives the copy on OpenShift its own name:

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: true
  targetNamespace: $CLASS_ID
  provider:
    source:      { name: $SRC, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: $SRC-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: $SRC-storage,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - { name: $VM, targetName: $VM-warm-cli }
EOF
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # READY True (Ctrl-C)

Start it: a Migration is what the console's Start button creates. A warm migration pre-copies until it has a cutover time:

oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN-run1, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOF
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # EXECUTING True (Ctrl-C)

In 2.4, after your start-warm-migration row, cut over by giving the Migration a cutover time of now:

oc -n openshift-mtv patch migration $PLAN-run1 --type merge -p "{\"spec\":{\"cutover\":\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\"}}"
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # SUCCEEDED True (Ctrl-C)

docs.title: 2.4 Inject, then cut over
docs.text:
Write the "start" row while your VM still runs on vSphere. It must survive the cutover:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'start-warm-migration', 'on vSphere, before cutover');"

Console (site A): Migration plans → d2-win-pg-s01 → Cutover → keep the date and time it offers (now) → Set cutover.

MTV now shuts your VM down on vSphere, takes one last snapshot, copies the small change since the last round, converts the drivers (virt-v2v installs virtio and the QEMU guest agent, and removes VMware Tools) and creates your VM on OpenShift.

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -w                        # SUCCEEDED True (Ctrl-C to stop watching)

✅ The plan shows Succeeded.

docs.title: 2.5 Review your VM on OpenShift
docs.text:
Console (site A): Virtualization → VirtualMachines, project student-01-0024-012 → win-pg-s01-warm.

Tab What you see Configuration → Network one NIC on default/vmnet23: your VLAN's bridge, so it keeps its address Configuration → Storage three disks on ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (ODF) 
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vm win-pg-s01-warm -o jsonpath='{range .spec.template.spec.networks[*]}{.multus.networkName}{"\n"}{end}'   # default/vmnet23
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmi win-pg-s01-warm -w                 # Running (Ctrl-C to stop watching)

Your VM was running on vSphere when it was cut over, so MTV starts it on OpenShift. If it shows Stopped, start it: Actions → Start [verify].

On the VM's Overview, the Guest agent shows as connected, and IP addresses shows 10.101.23.101.

✅ Running, guest agent connected, address 10.101.23.101.

docs.title: 2.6 Inject: the migration is complete, read back, and measure the outage
docs.text:
Give Windows a minute to start PostgreSQL, then:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'warm-migration-complete', 'on OpenShift site A');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ The read-back ends with demo-started, the 500 warm-precopy-load rows (written while the disks copied), start-warm-migration (the last row on vSphere) and warm-migration-complete (written on OpenShift). ovedr_verify shows chain_ok = t: nothing written during the copy was lost, changed or reordered.

The real outage. Your VM's heartbeat writer adds a row every 5 seconds, so the outage is the gap in it after your start-warm-migration row:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT ts AS back_at, date_trunc('second', gap) AS outage FROM (SELECT ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap FROM heartbeat) g WHERE gap > interval '10 seconds' AND ts > (SELECT max(ts) FROM marks WHERE student = 'student-01-0024-012' AND stage = 'start-warm-migration') ORDER BY ts;"

✅ One row: the cutover outage. Compare it with how long the first pre-copy took. A cold migration would have been down for all of that copy.

The guest tools were swapped:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -x -c "SELECT ts, platform, vmtools, qemu_ga, virtio FROM guest_tools ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1;"

✅ qemu_ga is Running, virtio lists the network and disk drivers, and vmtools is not running.

That is the end of Demo 2. Your VM moved to OpenShift Virtualization while it kept writing, and stopped only for the cutover.

💡 One copy on your VLAN at a time. If you did Demo 1, your project now holds two VMs, win-pg-s01 (stopped) and win-pg-s01-warm (running), with the same address. Never run both at once.

docs.title: Without VDDK: the paths Red Hat offers
docs.text:
Red Hat's current position (from Red Hat, 2026-10-14) on the VDDK dependency and the paths forward:

Path Status What it means An existing VDDK copy may remain a technical option If you already have a VDDK package that matches your VMware environment, it may still work. You are responsible for confirming your right to keep and use the software; Red Hat can then assess its technical suitability. Warm migration without VDDK Developer Preview There is no generally available warm path without VDDK today. Red Hat is testing an additional VDDK-independent transfer in MTV, designed to give comparable function for both warm and cold migration. Developer Preview means controlled evaluation, not production use. Cold migration without VDDK: storage copy offload generally available (MTV 2.11) MTV copies the disks through the storage array instead of through VDDK. GA for cold migrations, with supported storage appliances and configurations only.

What to do in your environment: qualify your datastore mix, storage design and timeline with Red Hat to pick the right path. Storage copy offload depends on your array: check it against Red Hat's list of supported appliances before you plan on it. This lab's datastores are NFS and haven't been qualified for it, so the lab's cold migration (Demo 1) uses MTV's default path (disks read over vCenter/ESXi HTTPS, no VDDK, slower).

Public references:

  • MTV 2.11: Planning VMware migrations and storage copy offload

docs.title: Addendum: how the lab staged this demo, as code
docs.text:
The provider, the maps and the CI pipeline are the same as Demo 1's (Demo 1 addendum). A warm migration needs three more things, and CI declares each one:

CI job Code What it declares for warm mtv-install Ansible role mtv_operator the pre-copy interval: 5 minutes instead of MTV's default 60, so a class sees several rounds vddk automation/customize/vddk.sh the VDDK image: Broadcom's library, which can't be redistributed, built from the lab's private copy into the cluster's own registry, then set on the provider (Lab S §S.15) stage automation/customize/stage.sh the warm plan d2-<vm>, landing as <vm>-warm. Staged and reported, never fatal: it waits for CBT, which you turn on in 2.2 
# the pre-copy interval, on MTV's own controller
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: ForkliftController
metadata: { name: forklift-controller, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  controller_precopy_interval: "5"        # minutes between pre-copy rounds
---
# the provider, plus the VDDK image (the only difference from Demo 1's)
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  type: vsphere
  url: https://vcenter01.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/sdk
  secret: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  settings:
    vddkInitImage: image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/openshift-mtv/vddk:8.0.3
---
# the staged warm plan: warm: true, and a target name so it never collides with Demo 1's copy
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: d2-win-pg-s01, namespace: openshift-mtv, labels: { ovedr/stage: plan, ovedr/type: warm } }
spec:
  warm: true
  targetNamespace: student-01-0024-012
  provider: { source: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map:
    network: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-storage,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms: [ { name: win-pg-s01, targetName: win-pg-s01-warm } ]

What stays a hands-on step, on purpose: CBT (2.2). It's a setting on the VMware VM, which the lab could set too (govc vm.change -e ctkEnabled=TRUE …), but turning it on yourself is the lesson. Then the Migration and its cutover (2.3, 2.4).

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o yaml
oc -n openshift-mtv get provider ovedr-vcenter01 -o jsonpath='{.spec.settings}{"\n"}'
